title: Accumulation of Trehalose 6-Phosphate in Candidozyma auris results in Decreased Echinocandin Resistance and Tolerance

paper_content.abstract: Candidozyma auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen that poses a major public-health challenge owing to high mortality and the limited efficacy of current therapies. Echinocandins, which inhibit β-glucan synthesis, are first-line therapy for invasive C. auris infection; however, resistance to this class is rising, underscoring the urgent need for new antifungal targets. Here we show that enzymes in the trehalose-biosynthetic pathway regulate stress responses, antifungal resistance/tolerance and virulence in C. auris. The tps2Δ strain displays heightened susceptibility to echinocandins, whereas tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains show resistance and tolerance comparable to wild type (WT). Mechanistically, the tps2Δ strain accumulates trehalose 6-phosphate (T6P), which inhibits hexokinase activity and reduces the flux of glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) into the chitin biosynthesis pathway, leading to substantially decreased cell wall chitin. During echinocandin exposure, the tps2Δ strain fails to compensate for reduced β-glucan with increased chitin, thereby rendering it highly susceptible to these drugs. In a systemic mouse infection model, deletion of the TPS2 gene results in lower tissue fungal burdens after treatment with caspofungin. Together, these findings identify Tps2 as a potential therapeutic target that can potentiate echinocandin efficacy in C. auris via a distinct mechanism of action.
paper_content.introduction:
Candidozyma auris is an emerging opportunistic pathogen known for its ability to colonize the skin and cause life-threatening systemic infections, particularly in hospitalized patients with underlying health conditions, including those affected by COVID-191,2. What makes C. auris particularly concerning is its frequent resistance to multiple classes of antifungal drugs, including azoles, polyenes, and echinocandins, which significantly complicates treatment3,4. Studies have shown that up to 90% of C. auris isolates exhibit resistance to fluconazole, 50% to amphotericin B, and 5% to echinocandins5,6. In vivo studies indicate that micafungin, an echinocandin, is more effective in treating invasive C. auris infections compared to fluconazole or amphotericin B7. However, the widespread use of these echinocandins has raised concerns about the potential development of resistance and tolerance to this critical class of antifungal drugs8–11. Here, resistance is considered as a decrease in susceptibility—i.e., an increased MIC relative to a control or clinical breakpoint—caused by stable genetic changes that alter the drug target and/or intracellular drug concentration. In contrast, tolerance is the ability of a otherwise drug-susceptible isolate to survive and grow slowly at concentrations above the MIC without a change in MIC. Tolerance reflects phenotypic heterogeneity and is typically mediated by central stress-response pathways12.

During infection, C. auris faces numerous stressors, including temperature fluctuations, nutrient and osmolarity changes, and hypoxic or oxidative stress, all of which can impact its survival and virulence13–15. The yeast must efficiently mobilize its energy reserves and protect its proteins against these damaging insults. Notably, the disaccharide trehalose has been implicated in providing protection against these stresses, playing a crucial role in the survival mechanisms of yeast under hostile conditions. Understanding the molecular basis of these protective strategies in C. auris is essential for developing new therapeutic approaches to combat this formidable pathogen16–18.

Trehalose (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside) is a non-reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond and is synthesized by a wide range of organisms, including bacteria, fungi, plants, and invertebrates17,19. However, trehalose is notably absent in mammals. In pathogenic fungi, trehalose plays a crucial role in cellular protection and stabilizing membranes under various stress conditions encountered during infection, including oxidative stress, osmotic stress and heat shock11. In addition, the protective effects of trehalose are also attributed to its ability to stabilize proteins by preventing their denaturation and aggregation20–23. Moreover, trehalose aids in the reactivation of denatured proteins by facilitating their interaction with molecular chaperones, such as heat shock proteins24. In addition to its protective functions, trehalose has been proposed to act as a reserve carbon source25. The biosynthesis of trehalose is governed by a two-step enzymatic pathway26. The first enzyme, Tps1, catalyzes the conversion of uridine diphosphate glucose (UDPG) and glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) into trehalose 6-phosphate (T6P). This T6P has been implicated in the regulation of hexokinase II, which in turn influences glycolytic flux in fungi27–29. In the next step, the second enzyme, Tps2, removes the phosphate group from T6P to produce trehalose. This biosynthetic pathway is absent in humans, making it an attractive target for the development of novel antifungal therapies25,30. Targeting the trehalose biosynthesis pathway in fungi could disrupt key stress responses and virulence mechanisms25, thereby providing a means for combating fungal infections with potentially minimal off-target effects in humans.

In this study, we investigated the role of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway in drug resistance and pathogenicity of C. auris. Our findings highlight the importance of trehalose biosynthetic enzymes in supporting fungal growth under thermal stress and in modulating antifungal drug responses. We found that the accumulation of T6P plays a critical role in inhibiting hexokinase activity, thereby reducing glycolytic flux and impairing cell wall biosynthesis. This disruption compromises the cell’s ability to compensate for echinocandin-induced cell wall damage, leading to decreased antifungal resistance and tolerance. These findings highlight Tps2 as a promising target for antifungal drug development.
paper_content.results:
Tps2 is important for heat and cell wall stress in C. auris
To assess the role of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway during growth of C. auris, we generated single-gene deletion mutants of TPS1 (tps1Δ) and TPS2 (tps2Δ), as well as a double mutant (tps1Δ tps2Δ), in the clade I reference strain B8441. Growth curve assays were performed in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with either 0.2% or 2% glucose. Unlike what has been observed in other yeast species31–33, disruption of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway in a C. auris clade I strain did not impact growth under physiological glucose concentrations, as all mutant strains (tps1Δ, tps2Δ, and tps1Δ tps2Δ) exhibited growth profiles comparable to the WT strain under both glucose concentrations (Fig. 1A). These results highlight a distinct metabolic feature of C. auris and indicate that trehalose biosynthesis is not essential for its glucose metabolism or overall growth under these tested conditions.

Given the established role of trehalose in mediating environmental stress responses, we evaluated the growth and stress susceptibility of the trehalose biosynthesis-deficient strains under various conditions. To assess thermal stress tolerance, growth assays were conducted at 37, 39, and 42°C. All mutant strains exhibited varying degrees of growth inhibition, with the tps2Δ strain exhibiting the most severe defect. Specifically, tps2Δ displayed impaired growth at 39°C and completely failed to grow at 42°C, indicating a marked loss of high-temperature tolerance (Fig. 1B). In contrast, although the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains also exhibited reduced growth relative to the WT at 42°C, their growth was less affected than that of the tps2Δ strain. These results suggest that trehalose synthesis plays a critical role in maintaining thermal stress tolerance in C. auris.

To evaluate stress resistance, the mutant and WT strains were tested against oxidative stress (hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂), osmotic stress (sodium chloride, NaCl), membrane stress (sodium dodecyl sulfate, SDS), and cell wall stress (calcofluor white, CFW, and Congo red, CR). No significant differences were detected between the WT and mutant strains under oxidative, osmotic, or membrane stress conditions (Fig. 1C). In contrast, clear differences emerged under cell wall stress. The tps2Δ strain showed increased sensitivity to CFW, a chitin-binding dye, but exhibited enhanced resistance to CR, which binds to β-glucan in the cell wall. By comparison, tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains did not display significant differences in sensitivity to either CFW or CR relative to the WT strain (Fig. 1C).

To quantitatively assess stress resistance, we calculated the area under the growth curve (AUC) for each condition and normalized these values to the WT strain to obtain relative resistance values (RRAUC), with the WT defined as 1. Values above 1 indicate greater resistance than WT, while values below 1 indicate reduced resistance. The relative ratios (RR) of AUC were calculated in Eq. 1:

RRAUC = AUC(mutant strain) / AUC(WT) (1)

These values are summarized in a heatmap (Fig. 1D). The tps2Δ strain exhibited reduced resistance to CFW and H₂O₂, but increased resistance to CR compared with the WT strain. In contrast, both tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains showed decreased resistance to both CFW and CR relative to the WT strain.

To confirm that the observed phenotypes were attributable to loss of the TPS2 gene, we complemented the tps2Δ strain to generate a TPS2-reintegrant strain (tps2Δ+TPS2). Complementation restored the stress-associated growth phenotypes: thermotolerance returned to WT levels, and resistance to the cell wall stressors CFW and CR was largely indistinguishable from the WT strain (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Tps2 plays a role in echinocandin resistance and tolerance
Given the trehalose biosynthetic pathway is involved in cell wall stress response, we investigated its contribution to resistance against clinically relevant antifungal drugs, which target either the fungal cell membrane (azoles and polyenes) or the cell wall (echinocandins). We conducted drug broth microdilution assays (BDA) (Fig. 2A, B) and ETEST® assays (Fig. 2C) to determine resistance and tolerance towards these drugs.

In this context, reduced relative resistance is interpreted as increased susceptibility compared with the WT strain, while tolerance refers to the ability of a subpopulation of cells to grow slowly but persistently at drug concentrations above the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Together, these assays allowed us to evaluate both resistance and tolerance phenotypes in the trehalose-deficient mutants.

Results from the BDAs revealed that deletion of the TPS2 gene significantly reduced resistance and tolerance to all three echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin). This is evident from respectively lower MIC and reduced growth at concentrations above the MIC (supra-MIC growth), quantified by lower AUC of the BDA (Fig. 2A). RRAUC calculated from the growth curves serve as an indicator of drug tolerance, which is visualized in the heatmap (Fig. 2B). The tps2Δ strain displayed a complete loss of tolerance to all three echinocandins and slightly increased tolerance to fluconazole. Meanwhile, the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains showed a slight increase in tolerance to amphotericin B.

Consistent with the phenotypic observations, Etest analysis demonstrated a clear reduction in echinocandin resistance and tolerance in the tps2Δ strain compared to the WT. The MIC values for all three echinocandins were lower in the tps2Δ strain than in the WT, indicating increased susceptibility. The specific MIC values are shown in the upper right corner of each Etest. Furthermore, the tps2Δ strain exhibited minimal to no growth within the inhibition elipse after 48 h, reflecting a complete loss of echinocandin tolerance (Fig. 2C). In contrast, no significant differences in susceptibility or tolerance to amphotericin B or fluconazole were observed between the tps2Δ and WT strains.

To further establish that the phenotype stems from TPS2 gene loss, we assessed caspofungin susceptibility and tolerance in the TPS2 reintegrant strain (tps2Δ+TPS2) using BDA and Etest assays (Supplementary Fig. S2). Complementation restored WT behavior: the caspofungin MIC of tps2Δ+TPS2 matched WT, and supra-MIC growth was likewise comparable. These results confirm that the heightened echinocandin sensitivity of the tps2Δ strain is due to TPS2 gene deficiency.

T6P accumulation in the tps2Δ strain is independent of caspofungin treatment
To investigate whether intracellular levels of trehalose and T6P influence echinocandin resistance and tolerance in C. auris, we quantified these metabolites in exponentially growing cells, both in the presence and absence of caspofungin (Fig. 3A, B). In unstressed conditions, deletion of the TPS2 gene led to a substantial accumulation of T6P, reaching levels nearly 300-fold higher than those observed in the WT strain. Conversely, deletion of the TPS1 gene, either alone or in combination with the TPS2 gene, resulted in a complete loss of detectable trehalose or T6P. Interestingly, deletion of the TPS2 gene alone still results in low accumulation of a small, residual amount of trehalose, similar to what is observed in C. albicans and C. glabrata31.

To assess whether trehalose or T6P levels respond to echinocandin stress, exponentially growing cells were treated with caspofungin at ten times MIC (2.5 µg/mL) for 60 min. However, no significant changes in trehalose or T6P levels were observed in either the WT or mutant strains following treatment (Fig. 3A, B). It is interesting to note that in the WT under normal conditions, there is already a high amount of trehalose produced. This is different to e.g., the situation in S. cerevisiae, where in exponentially grown cells, there is nearly no accumulation of trehalose34. This difference may be responsible for the intrinsically very high stress tolerance of C. auris.

Tps2 exhibits conserved roles across distinct C. auris clades
To assess whether the role of the trehalose synthesis pathway is conserved across different clades of C. auris, we performed a phylogenetic analysis of the Tps2 proteins (Fig. 4A), which revealed that Tps2 is highly conserved across all five C. auris clades, with minimal sequence divergence. To further investigate the functional conservation of the TPS2 gene, we generated TPS2 gene deletion strains in representative strains from Clade III (B11221), Clade IV (B11244), and Clade V (IFRC2087). Clade II was excluded from this analysis, given that Clade II strains are rarely associated with systemic infections and echinocandin treatment35.

The resulting tps2Δ strains from different C. auris clades were analyzed using drug and stress BDAs to assess their responses to diverse antifungal treatments and environmental stresses. From the drug BDA assay (Fig. 4B), all tps2Δ strains exhibited reduced MIC values for three echinocandins compared to their respective WT strain. The stress-response phenotypes observed in these tps2Δ strains were also largely consistent with those observed for the Clade I strain B8441. Specifically, deletion of the TPS2 gene resulted in increased sensitivity to CFW and enhanced resistance to CR, indicating alterations in cell wall stress responses.

To further quantify differences in stress and drug tolerance, relative resistance was assessed by calculating the area under the curve (RRAUC) for each condition (Fig. 4C). Across all clades, tps2Δ strains showed a marked reduction in RRAUC values for echinocandins. For CR stress, RRAUC values increased in all tps2Δ strains, while under CFW stress, RRAUC values decreased, further supporting a shift in cell wall composition and stress response. These findings demonstrate that the function of Tps2 in supporting echinocandin resistance and tolerance and maintaining cell wall integrity is conserved across multiple C. auris clades.

Deletion of the TPS2 gene results in impaired chitin biosynthesis
To investigate the mechanism underlying the increased echinocandin susceptibility of the tps2Δ strain, we compared cell-wall composition in the WT Clade I isolate B8441 and the corresponding panel of Clade I mutant strains. Confocal microscopy was performed to visualize specific components of the cell wall, employing CFW to detect chitin, Alexa Fluor 488–conjugated antibodies to stain β-glucans, and Concanavalin A–Alexa Fluor 488 to visualize mannans (Fig. 5A). The confocal microscopy images revealed significantly reduced CFW staining intensity in the tps2Δ strain. In contrast, no significant differences in outer cell membrane mannan and β-glucan levels were detected between the tps2Δ and WT strains. The cell wall stainings of tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains showed no notable differences compared to WT cells, indicating no significant alterations in chitin, β-glucan, or mannan content.

To further substantiate the microscopy findings, we quantified the same three major cell wall components using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). These data confirmed a significant reduction in chitin content in the tps2Δ strain compared to the WT (Fig. 5B). In contrast, mannan and β-glucan levels remained comparable across all strains.

The observed reduction in chitin content in the tps2Δ strain prompted us to investigate basal expression levels of genes involved in fungal cell wall biosynthesis (Fig. 6A). To this end, we examined the expression of several putative chitin synthase genes (CHS1, CHS2, CHS3, and CHS8) (Fig. 6B), as well as the GFA1 gene (Fig. 6C), which encodes glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase—an enzyme catalyzing the initial step in the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway essential for chitin synthesis. In addition, we assessed the expression of genes encoding β-glucan synthases (FKS1 and FKS2) to comprehensively evaluate cell wall biosynthesis alterations in mutant strains (Fig. 6D).

Quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed significant alterations, primarily within the chitin biosynthesis pathway. Notably, GFA1 expression was significantly increased in all mutant strains relative to the WT, underscoring a critical link between trehalose metabolism and chitin biosynthesis. Conversely, CHS1 and CHS2 genes expression levels were significantly decreased in the tps2Δ strain, while expression levels of CHS3 and CHS8 genes remained unchanged across all strains. Furthermore, expression of FKS1 and FKS2 genes showed no significant differences, suggesting that β-glucan synthesis was unaffected by TPS1 or TPS2 gene disruption. Collectively, these results are consistent with and support the observed reduction in chitin content specifically observed in the tps2Δ strain.

Gfa1 is essential but does not account for the tps2Δ echinocandin susceptibility
Gene expression assays revealed that GFA1 gene expression was upregulated in the tps2Δ strain. Based on this observation, we initially hypothesized that T6P accumulation in the tps2Δ background may directly alter the structure or enzymatic activity of Gfa1, thereby impairing chitin synthesis and compromising cell wall integrity, ultimately rendering the cells more susceptible to echinocandin-induced stress. To test this hypothesis, we generated a GFA1 gene knockout strain in the B8441 background and assessed its phenotype using BDA and Etest analysis. Growth curve analysis demonstrated that Gfa1 is essential for viability with glucose as a carbon source in C. auris, as deletion mutants were unable to grow in glucose-containing media (Fig. 7A). The restoration of growth upon supplementation with exogenous glucosamine confirmed that the growth defect was attributable to impaired hexosamine biosynthesis. Notably, when glucosamine was provided at a minimal concentration (10 mM) sufficient to support basal growth, the gfa1Δ strain exhibited substantially reduced resistance and tolerance to caspofungin (Fig. 7B, C). Increasing the concentration of glucosamine progressively improved both resistance and tolerance; however, full recovery to WT levels was not achieved. These findings indicate that the accumulation of T6P does not directly alter the structure or enzymatic function of Gfa1.

T6P accumulation indirectly reduces chitin production by inhibiting hexokinase activity
To investigate how the deletion of the TPS2 gene affects the chitin synthesis pathway, we focused on the role of T6P, a known regulator of the initial steps of glycolysis in yeast, primarily through its inhibition of hexokinase II (Fig. 8A)36. To assess whether this is also the case for C. auris, we analyzed hexokinase enzymatic activity in WT and mutant strains. Both the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains exhibited increased hexokinase activity, while deletion of the TPS2 gene resulted in a significant reduction in hexokinase activity compared to the WT strain (Fig. 8B). Complementation of TPS2 gene restored hexokinase activity to WT levels (Supplementary Fig. S3).

Considering that the trehalose biosynthesis pathway modulates glycolytic flux in various fungal species, we subsequently measured metabolites derived from glucose-dependent pathways. Therefore, 13C NMR spectroscopy was conducted to elucidate the interplay between glycolysis, trehalose metabolism, and chitin synthesis (Fig. 8C–F). The analysis revealed that the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains exhibited an increased and quicker glucose consumption compared to the WT (Fig. 8C). This is similar to what is observed in S. cerevisiae, where a tps1Δ strain has a very high flux into glycolysis because of very high hexokinase activity. As a result of this higher influx in glycolysis, both the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains produced ethanol at a higher rate compared to the WT (Fig. 8D), while glycerol and mannitol levels remained unchanged (Fig. 8E, F). In contrast, the tps2Δ strain exhibited a pronounced reduction in glucose consumption (Fig. 7C), accompanied by significantly lower levels of glycolysis-derived metabolites, including ethanol, glycerol, and mannitol. As a result, reduced carbon flow through glycolysis may limit the availability of F6P for downstream biosynthetic pathways. Given that UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), the precursor for chitin synthesis, is derived from F6P, these findings also imply that chitin biosynthesis is compromised in the tps2Δ strain. This metabolic constraint likely explains the reduced chitin levels detected in the tps2Δ strain. 13C NMR spectroscopy also confirmed the synthesis of trehalose for the WT and accumulation of T6P for the tps2Δ strain (Supplementary Fig. S4).

Exogenous glucosamine restores caspofungin resistance and tolerance in the tps2Δ strain
To determine whether the reduced resistance and tolerance of the tps2Δ strain to echinocandins were directly attributable to T6P accumulation, resulting in impaired glycolytic flux and subsequently diminished chitin biosynthesis, we performed caspofungin susceptibility assays with varying concentrations of exogenous glucosamine to evaluate its potential to rescue the susceptibility phenotype. The results demonstrated a non-linear relationship between glucosamine concentration and caspofungin resistance. Specifically, the MIC values of the tps2Δ strain were approximately 0.125 µg/mL at 10 mM, 0.25 µg/mL at 20 mM, and 1 µg/mL at both 30 mM and 50 mM glucosamine. These data suggest that low to moderate levels of glucosamine partially restore caspofungin tolerance in the absence of the TPS2 gene (Fig. 9A).

Consistent with the BDA findings, Etest assays performed after 48 h confirmed that glucosamine supplementation improved caspofungin resistance and tolerance in the tps2Δ strain, but this improvement did not continue beyond 30 mM. At both 30 mM and 50 mM glucosamine, the tps2Δ strain exhibited similar capacity for growth within the inhibition ellipse (Fig. 9B). Together, these results suggest that while glucosamine can compensate to some extent for the loss of the TPS2 gene, its ability to enhance caspofungin resistance and tolerance is limited and does not increase indefinitely with concentration.

Deletion of Tps2 sensitizes C. auris to caspofungin in a murine candidemia model
Given the pronounced defects in echinocandin resistance and tolerance observed in the tps2Δ strain under in vitro conditions, we determined whether these phenotypes translated to differences in susceptibility in an in vivo context. To assess the impact of the tps2Δ strain on the in vivo susceptibility of C. auris to caspofungin, immunocompromised mice were intravenously infected with either the WT strain or the tps2Δ strain and subsequently treated with caspofungin or PBS. To assess the virulence of C. auris strains and the therapeutic impact of caspofungin, we measured fungal burden in the kidneys and brains of infected mice, as schematically depicted in Fig. 10A. To assess the health status of mice after infection and treatment, body weight was monitored daily from day 0 to day 6 (Fig. 10B). No significant differences in body weight were observed among the groups, regardless of infection with WT or tps2Δ strains, or treatment with PBS or caspofungin. Further, we found that in the absence of caspofungin treatment, both the WT and tps2Δ strains showed similar levels of fungal burden in these organs, indicating that deletion of the TPS2 gene does not impair the intrinsic virulence of C. auris. However, following caspofungin treatment, fungal burden in mice infected with the tps2Δ cells was significantly lower than in those infected with the WT strain in both kidneys and brains (Fig. 10C). This indicates that tps2Δ cells are less able to survive after caspofungin treatment in vivo. Together, these findings suggest that loss of the TPS2 gene leads to a complete loss of caspofungin tolerance under host conditions and that a combination therapy of echinocandin with a Tps2 inhibitor would be an effective combination therapy.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This is a really interesting paper where the authors provide convincing in vitro and in vivo evidence that deletion of TSP2 in
C. auris enhances the susceptibility of C. auris to echinocandins. This indeed suggests that targeting Tsp2 may be a useful
strategy to enhance susceptibility of C. auris to echinocandins. I think is definitely something worth pursuing as this multi-
drug resistant fungal pathogen continues to spread around the globe.
My concerns are these:
1. When I think about echinocandin tolerance and resistance related specifically to chitin, I attribute tolerance to the natural
variations in amount of chitin in the cell walls of cells in a population (i.e. those cells with a naturally high chitin content will
be tolerant), but resistance arises due to a stress-induced compensatory increase in cell wall chitin that only occurs when
cells are treated with a non-lethal dose of echinocandin.
Although the authors show that deletion of TSP2 results in the accumulation of T6P, inhibition hexokinase, reduced flux
through glycolysis, decreased chitin content, and increased susceptibility to echinocandins, they have not actually provided
direct evidence that “the inability to compensate the reduction in β-glucan levels with increased chitin production during
echinocandin treatment in the tsp2Δ strain rendered this strain highly susceptible to these drugs” (line 39-41). Does
treatment of C. auris with a sub-MIC of echinocandin result in a compensatory increase in cell wall chitin? Is this
compensatory increase no longer observed in a tsp2 mutant?
2. A decrease in chitin content typically renders cells less susceptible to CFW, not more susceptible. I am therefore finding it
difficult to reconcile the phenotype of the tsp2Δ mutant in relation the chitin content and susceptibility to CFW (line 224-226).
Could the increased susceptibility of the tsp2 mutant to CFW (compared to wildtype) be related more to general stress
protection provided by trehalose, rather than chitin?
3. To my knowledge, the function of the C. auris chitin synthases and their regulation has not yet been investigated.
However, in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, the class IV chitin synthase (Chs3) makes the majority of cell wall chitin. I would
therefore be very cautious of making a statement that decreased CHS1 and CHS2 transcripts in the tsp2 mutant
(compared to wild type) indicate impaired chitin biosynthesis capacity (line 239).
Minor comments:
4. The section “Loss of Tsp2 impairs echinocandin resistance and tolerance via T6P accumulation” (line 163) simply shows
that T6P accumulates in the tsp2Δ mutant. The link with echinocandin susceptibility has not yet been established. Perhaps
the subheading could be re-worded?
5. Line 195 and 197: The reference to Figure 1A is incorrect.
6. Growth phenotype assay (line 546). What volume of culture was added to each well in the 96 well plate? What software
was used for the analysis of the growth curves?
7. The colour and symbol legends in Figures 1 and 2 indicate three tsp1 mutants (-1, -2 and -3), three tsp2 mutants and three
tsp1tsp2 mutants. Do these refer to biological replicates? Ideally, OD600 should be plotted on a log scale so that the curves
better represent the phases of growth.
8. Figure 5B: Are the labels on the y-axes correct?

logical line of enquiry and makes steps to understand the underpinning mechanisms contributing to the observed
phenotypes. The study is highly relevant and novel and is of importance given the widespread drug resistance of this
recently emerged pathogen. It also directly links drug tolerance with cell wall composition and metabolic flux and clearly
demonstrates the importance of TPS2 in antifungal susceptibility.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This tightly reasoned report presents mechanistic insight into the emerging pathogen Candida auris' insensitivity to
echinocandin antifungals. Candida auris has become an increasing menace over the last decade due to its resilience to
antifungals and disinfectants, so on that basis the study is highly significant. Moreover, the findings point to an enzyme with
a causal role, and in this way the authors have a druggable target. This element of the study further increases its
significance.
A second strength of the study is the thoroughness of the analysis. For example, strains from all four major pathogenic C.
auris clades are tested. Also, metabolic inferences are pursued and validated with metabolomic characterization. Finally, a
point that all readers will appreciate is the simplicity of the explanation at which the authors arrive. It is the kind of outcome
that even students in my Introductory Microbiology class could understand and appreciate! In fact, if this work is published in
time, I may even include it in a lecture this fall.
The one minor experimental criticism that I have is that the most revealing mutant, the tps2Δ strain, was not complemented.
There was a G418 marker developed by Santana and O'Meara in Nat Commun. 2021 Dec 10;12(1):7197 that might be
useful, or the authors could recycle their NAT marker as they do for other purposes. I do not doubt the overall
phenotypic results as they stand - the authors make the mutant in multiple strains, for example - but for some of the findings,
such as reduced chitin accumulation and reduced hexokinase activity, complementation would ensure that the conclusions reach the
highest standard.
The one minor manuscript preparation criticism that I have is that the Discussion and Results sections seem to overlap more
than necessary. I wondered if the authors might benefit from merging the two into a single "Results and Discussion" format.
This issue is more of a matter of taste though, which is why I consider it quite minor.
My one strong recommendation with regard to manuscript preparation is that the authors should define clearly what
resistance and tolerance each mean. These are terms with distinctions that can be a little hazy among a broad audience. I
am 99% certain that the authors' assays are completely in line with the simple definitions that I always refer to
(Berman and Krysan, Nat Rev Microbiol. 2020 Jun;18(6):319-331), so I do not question the authors' assays and conclusions;
my recommendation is really to make sure the work can be appreciated by a broad readership.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. As for the first question (Does treatment
of C. auris with a sub-MIC of echinocandin result in a compensatory increase in cell wall
chitin? ). Yes — C. auris, similar to other Candida species, is capable of mounting a
compensatory increase in cell wall chitin in response to echinocandin treatment at sub-
inhibitory concentrations. This adaptive response is a well-established mechanism of
echinocandin tolerance, as it helps maintain cell wall integrity when β-1,3-glucan synthesis is
impaired. Notably, Lara-Aguilar et al. (2021) demonstrated that C. auris exhibits a significant
increase in chitin content following exposure to high concentrations of caspofungin.
Although this response is less pronounced compared to C. albicans, it supports the presence
of a conserved, stress-induced chitin remodeling mechanism in C. auris that contributes to
survival under echinocandin pressure.
To directly address the reviewer’s questions, we measured chitin levels after sub-MIC
caspofungin treatment in WT and tps2Δ strains. Exponentially growing cells were exposed to
¼ and ½ MIC caspofungin, stained with Calcofluor White, and analyzed by confocal
microscopy. Sub-MIC caspofungin increased chitin in WT cells, and a comparable increase
was observed in the tps2Δ mutant. Thus, the compensatory chitin response to echinocandin
stress is largely Tps2-independent. At higher (supra-MIC) concentrations, tps2Δ growth was
markedly inhibited, precluding reliable chitin assessment.
We have incorporated these new data and discussion into the revised manuscript (new
Figure S5; revised text, lines 493–495 (in clean manuscript)).
In parallel, we have observed that supplementation with exogenous glucosamine — a
precursor in the chitin biosynthesis pathway — increases caspofungin resistance and
tolerance in both wild-type and tps2Δ strains. These results clarify that the
hypersusceptibility of tps2Δ is unlikely due to a failure to trigger chitin remodeling, but
rather is consistent with a metabolic limitation (reduced glycolytic flux/precursor supply)
that compromises cell-wall robustness under drug stress.
2. A decrease in chitin content typically renders cells less susceptible to CFW, not more
susceptible. I am therefore finding it difficult to reconcile the phenotype of the tsp2Δ
mutant in relation the chitin content and susceptibility to CFW (line 224-226). Could the
increased susceptibility of the tsp2 mutant to CFW (compared to wildtype) be related more
to general stress protection provided by trehalose, rather than chitin?
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that the phenotype of
tps2Δ—lower chitin content yet heightened sensitivity to calcofluor white (CFW)—does not
follow the usual correlation between total chitin levels and CFW susceptibility. Consistent
with previous reports 1-3, our data suggest that CFW sensitivity depends on chitin
accessibility and overall cell-wall organization, not simply on chitin abundance4. We have
revised the text to clarify this distinction.
We also considered whether loss of the stress-protective function of trehalose could explain
the phenotype. However, both tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains, which are similarly defective
in trehalose biosynthesis, do not display increased CFW sensitivity compared with the wild
type (Figure 1C,D). This argues against trehalose depletion as the main cause.
Instead, we propose that accumulation of trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) in tps2Δ disrupts
cell-wall architecture—for example, by altering β-glucan–chitin cross-linking and increasing
wall porosity—thereby exposing the remaining chitin to CFW and leading to hypersensitivity
despite the overall reduction in chitin content.
3. To my knowledge, the function of the C. auris chitin synthases and their regulation has
not yet been investigated. However, in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, the class IV chitin
synthase (Chs3) makes the majority of cell wall chitin. I would therefore be very cautious of
making a statement that decreased CHS1 and CHS2 transcripts in the tsp2 mutant
(compared to wild type) indicate impaired chitin biosynthesis capacity (line 239).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this clarification. In our dataset, CHS1 and CHS2
transcripts were reduced in the tps2Δ mutant. While this pattern may suggest a general
down-regulation of the chitin-biosynthetic program, we agree that transcript levels alone do
not establish reduced chitin synthesis—especially since CHS3, the principal chitin synthase in
many Candida species, was unchanged. A plausible explanation is that Chs3 activity is
regulated mainly post-translationally. Accordingly, we have removed the over-interpretive
language from the Results (line 245) and now address potential transcriptional and post-
translational regulation of chitin-synthesis enzymes in the Discussion (lines 442–454).
Minor comments:
4. The section “Loss of Tsp2 impairs echinocandin resistance and tolerance via T6P
accumulation” (line 163) simply shows that T6P accumulates in the tsp2Δ mutant. The link
with echinocandin susceptibility has not yet been established. Perhaps the subheading could
be re-worded?
Response: We agree that the original subheading overstated the link between T6P
accumulation and echinocandin susceptibility. To better reflect the actual results presented
in this section, we have revised the subheading to:
“T6P accumulates in the tps2Δ strain independently of caspofungin treatment”
This wording more precisely describes our findings and avoids implying a causal link to
echinocandin susceptibility, which is addressed in subsequent sections.
5. Line 195 and 197: The reference to Figure 1A is incorrect.
Response: We have corrected the reference by removing the citation to Figure 1A. To clarify
the data presentation, we have revised Figures 4B and 4C to include the data for clade I WT
and clade I tps2Δ strains.
6. Growth phenotype assay (line 546). What volume of culture was added to each well in
the 96 well plate? What software was used for the analysis of the growth curves?
Response: We have revised the description in the Methods section to include this
information. Specifically, we now state that each well contained a total volume of 200 µL
(20 µL cell suspension + 180 µL medium), and that growth curve data were analyzed using
Graphpad Prism version 10.4.2.
7. The colour and symbol legends in Figures 1 and 2 indicate three tsp1 mutants (-1, -2 and -
3), three tsp2 mutants and three tsp1tsp2 mutants. Do these refer to biological replicates?
Ideally, OD600 should be plotted on a log scale so that the curves better represent the
phases of growth.
Response: In Figures 1 and 2, the “-1, -2, -3” labels represent independent biological
replicates (separately isolated tps1Δ, tps2Δ, and tps1Δ tps2Δ transformants), each derived
from distinct colonies and cultured independently. We have clarified this in the figure
legends section.
Y-axis scaling. We appreciate the suggestion to use a logarithmic y-axis. A log scale is ideal
when complete growth curves (lag, exponential, and stationary phases) are reliably
captured, as in erlenmeyers-based assays. In our study, OD₆₀₀ measurements were obtained
with a microplate reader (multiscan), whose dynamic range under our conditions did not
accurately capture the stationary phase. Because our analyses focus on the lag and early
exponential phases, a linear y-axis preserves visual resolution in the low-OD range, whereas
a log scale would compress these values without revealing additional phases. For these
reasons, we have retained the linear scaling.
In the reply to referee 2 we have added figures where we have put the Y axis in a log scale.
8. Figure 5B: Are the labels on the y-axes correct?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. As described in the Methods, chitin
levels were quantified as glucosamine equivalents, while β-glucan and mannan were
quantified as glucose and mannose equivalents, respectively. So the full y-axes should read
like: Chitin: µmol GlcN eq./mg wet weight) β-glucan: µmol Glc eq./ mg wet weight) Mannan:
µmol Man eq./mg wet weight).
To avoid cluttering the y-axis, we have kept the labels short (e.g. Chitin [µmol/mg ww]) and
added a clear explanation in the figure legend stating that the values represent
monosaccharide equivalents derived from standard curves. This ensures accuracy while
keeping the figure easy to read.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s point regarding the absence of reintegrant controls.
We did not include the reintegrant strain as we use three independent mutant

and figure references have been added to the manuscript (see Fig. S1–S3).

To assess the role of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway during growth of C. auris, we

Figure 1: Growth assays are usually reported with y-axis in log scale

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This tightly reasoned report presents mechanistic insight into the emerging pathogen
Candida auris' insensitivity to echinocandin antifungals. Candida auris has become an
increasing menace over the last decade due to its resilience to antifungals and disinfectants,
so on that basis the study is highly significant. Moreover, the findings point to an enzyme
with a causal role, and in this way the authors have a druggable target. This element of the
study further increases its significance.
A second strength of the study is the thoroughness of the analysis. For example, strains
from all four major pathogenic C. auris clades are tested. Also, metabolic inferences are
pursued and validated with metabolomic characterization. Finally, a point that all readers
will appreciate is the simplicity of the explanation at which the authors arrive. It is the kind
of outcome that even students in my Introductory Microbiology class could understand and
appreciate! In fact, if this work is published in time, I may even include it in a lecture this fall.
The one minor experimental criticism that I have is that the most revealing mutant, the
tps2Δ strain, was not complemented. There was a G418 marker developed by Santana and
O'Meara in Nat Commun. 2021 Dec 10;12(1):7197 that might be useful, or the authors could
recycle their NAT marker as they do for other purposes. I do not doubt the overall
phenotypic results as they stand - the authors make the mutant in multiple strains, for
example - but for some of the findings, such as reduced chitin accumulation and reduced
hexokinase activity, complementation would ensure that the conclusions reach the highest
standard.
The one minor manuscript preparation criticism that I have is that the Discussion and
Results sections seem to overlap more than necessary. I wondered if the authors might
benefit from merging the two into a single "Results and Discussion" format. This issue is
more of a matter of taste though, which is why I consider it quite minor.

method 5 and re-evaluated key phenotypes. Complementation restored wild-type behavior
across assays: thermotolerance, cell-wall stress responses (CFW and CR), caspofungin
susceptibility and tolerance (BDA/Etest) and hexokinase activity assay. These data
demonstrate that the phenotypes observed in tps2Δ are specifically attributable to loss of
TPS2. The new results and figure references have been added to the manuscript (see Fig.
S1–S5).
Thank you for noting the redundancy. We have streamlined the Discussion and Conclusion
by removing repetitive descriptions of results and consolidating overlapping passages. The
revised sections retain all key findings and interpretations while improving clarity and
readability.
My one strong recommendation with regard to manuscript preparation is that the authors
should define clearly what resistance and tolerance each mean. These are terms with
distinctions that can be a little hazy among a broad audience. I am 99% certain that the
authors' assays are completely in line with the simple definitions that I always refer to
(Berman and Krysan, Nat Rev Microbiol. 2020 Jun;18(6):319-331), so I do not question the
authors' assays and conclusions; my recommendation is really to make sure the work can be
appreciated by a broad readership.
Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have added explicit definitions of
resistance and tolerance (citing Berman & Krysan, Nat Rev Microbiol, 2020) to the
Introduction section, and we clarified them in the relevant figure legends (Figure 2).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Candidozyma auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen that poses a major public-health challenge owing to high mortality and the limited efficacy of current therapies. Echinocandins, which inhibit β-glucan synthesis, are first-line therapy for invasive C. auris infection; however, resistance to this class is rising, underscoring the urgent need for new antifungal targets. Here we show that enzymes in the trehalose-biosynthetic pathway regulate stress responses, antifungal resistance/tolerance and virulence in C. auris. The tps2Δ strain displays heightened susceptibility to echinocandins, whereas tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains show resistance and tolerance comparable to wild type (WT). Mechanistically, the tps2Δ strain accumulates trehalose 6-phosphate (T6P), which inhibits hexokinase activity and reduces the flux of glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) into the chitin biosynthesis pathway, leading to substantially decreased cell wall chitin. During echinocandin exposure, the tps2Δ strain fails to compensate for reduced β-glucan with increased chitin, thereby rendering it highly susceptible to these drugs. In a systemic mouse infection model, deletion of the TPS2 gene results in lower tissue fungal burdens after treatment with caspofungin. Together, these findings identify Tps2 as a potential therapeutic target that can potentiate echinocandin efficacy in C. auris via a distinct mechanism of action.

---

## Introduction

Candidozyma auris is an emerging opportunistic pathogen known for its ability to colonize the skin and cause life-threatening systemic infections, particularly in hospitalized patients with underlying health conditions, including those affected by COVID-191,2. What makes C. auris particularly concerning is its frequent resistance to multiple classes of antifungal drugs, including azoles, polyenes, and echinocandins, which significantly complicates treatment3,4. Studies have shown that up to 90% of C. auris isolates exhibit resistance to fluconazole, 50% to amphotericin B, and 5% to echinocandins5,6. In vivo studies indicate that micafungin, an echinocandin, is more effective in treating invasive C. auris infections compared to fluconazole or amphotericin B7. However, the widespread use of these echinocandins has raised concerns about the potential development of resistance and tolerance to this critical class of antifungal drugs8–11. Here, resistance is considered as a decrease in susceptibility—i.e., an increased MIC relative to a control or clinical breakpoint—caused by stable genetic changes that alter the drug target and/or intracellular drug concentration. In contrast, tolerance is the ability of a otherwise drug-susceptible isolate to survive and grow slowly at concentrations above the MIC without a change in MIC. Tolerance reflects phenotypic heterogeneity and is typically mediated by central stress-response pathways12.

During infection, C. auris faces numerous stressors, including temperature fluctuations, nutrient and osmolarity changes, and hypoxic or oxidative stress, all of which can impact its survival and virulence13–15. The yeast must efficiently mobilize its energy reserves and protect its proteins against these damaging insults. Notably, the disaccharide trehalose has been implicated in providing protection against these stresses, playing a crucial role in the survival mechanisms of yeast under hostile conditions. Understanding the molecular basis of these protective strategies in C. auris is essential for developing new therapeutic approaches to combat this formidable pathogen16–18.

Trehalose (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside) is a non-reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond and is synthesized by a wide range of organisms, including bacteria, fungi, plants, and invertebrates17,19. However, trehalose is notably absent in mammals. In pathogenic fungi, trehalose plays a crucial role in cellular protection and stabilizing membranes under various stress conditions encountered during infection, including oxidative stress, osmotic stress and heat shock11. In addition, the protective effects of trehalose are also attributed to its ability to stabilize proteins by preventing their denaturation and aggregation20–23. Moreover, trehalose aids in the reactivation of denatured proteins by facilitating their interaction with molecular chaperones, such as heat shock proteins24. In addition to its protective functions, trehalose has been proposed to act as a reserve carbon source25. The biosynthesis of trehalose is governed by a two-step enzymatic pathway26. The first enzyme, Tps1, catalyzes the conversion of uridine diphosphate glucose (UDPG) and glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) into trehalose 6-phosphate (T6P). This T6P has been implicated in the regulation of hexokinase II, which in turn influences glycolytic flux in fungi27–29. In the next step, the second enzyme, Tps2, removes the phosphate group from T6P to produce trehalose. This biosynthetic pathway is absent in humans, making it an attractive target for the development of novel antifungal therapies25,30. Targeting the trehalose biosynthesis pathway in fungi could disrupt key stress responses and virulence mechanisms25, thereby providing a means for combating fungal infections with potentially minimal off-target effects in humans.

In this study, we investigated the role of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway in drug resistance and pathogenicity of C. auris. Our findings highlight the importance of trehalose biosynthetic enzymes in supporting fungal growth under thermal stress and in modulating antifungal drug responses. We found that the accumulation of T6P plays a critical role in inhibiting hexokinase activity, thereby reducing glycolytic flux and impairing cell wall biosynthesis. This disruption compromises the cell’s ability to compensate for echinocandin-induced cell wall damage, leading to decreased antifungal resistance and tolerance. These findings highlight Tps2 as a promising target for antifungal drug development.

---

## Results

Tps2 is important for heat and cell wall stress in C. auris
To assess the role of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway during growth of C. auris, we generated single-gene deletion mutants of TPS1 (tps1Δ) and TPS2 (tps2Δ), as well as a double mutant (tps1Δ tps2Δ), in the clade I reference strain B8441. Growth curve assays were performed in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with either 0.2% or 2% glucose. Unlike what has been observed in other yeast species31–33, disruption of the trehalose biosynthesis pathway in a C. auris clade I strain did not impact growth under physiological glucose concentrations, as all mutant strains (tps1Δ, tps2Δ, and tps1Δ tps2Δ) exhibited growth profiles comparable to the WT strain under both glucose concentrations (Fig. 1A). These results highlight a distinct metabolic feature of C. auris and indicate that trehalose biosynthesis is not essential for its glucose metabolism or overall growth under these tested conditions.

Given the established role of trehalose in mediating environmental stress responses, we evaluated the growth and stress susceptibility of the trehalose biosynthesis-deficient strains under various conditions. To assess thermal stress tolerance, growth assays were conducted at 37, 39, and 42°C. All mutant strains exhibited varying degrees of growth inhibition, with the tps2Δ strain exhibiting the most severe defect. Specifically, tps2Δ displayed impaired growth at 39°C and completely failed to grow at 42°C, indicating a marked loss of high-temperature tolerance (Fig. 1B). In contrast, although the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains also exhibited reduced growth relative to the WT at 42°C, their growth was less affected than that of the tps2Δ strain. These results suggest that trehalose synthesis plays a critical role in maintaining thermal stress tolerance in C. auris.

To evaluate stress resistance, the mutant and WT strains were tested against oxidative stress (hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂), osmotic stress (sodium chloride, NaCl), membrane stress (sodium dodecyl sulfate, SDS), and cell wall stress (calcofluor white, CFW, and Congo red, CR). No significant differences were detected between the WT and mutant strains under oxidative, osmotic, or membrane stress conditions (Fig. 1C). In contrast, clear differences emerged under cell wall stress. The tps2Δ strain showed increased sensitivity to CFW, a chitin-binding dye, but exhibited enhanced resistance to CR, which binds to β-glucan in the cell wall. By comparison, tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains did not display significant differences in sensitivity to either CFW or CR relative to the WT strain (Fig. 1C).

To quantitatively assess stress resistance, we calculated the area under the growth curve (AUC) for each condition and normalized these values to the WT strain to obtain relative resistance values (RRAUC), with the WT defined as 1. Values above 1 indicate greater resistance than WT, while values below 1 indicate reduced resistance. The relative ratios (RR) of AUC were calculated in Eq. 1:

RRAUC = AUC(mutant strain) / AUC(WT) (1)

These values are summarized in a heatmap (Fig. 1D). The tps2Δ strain exhibited reduced resistance to CFW and H₂O₂, but increased resistance to CR compared with the WT strain. In contrast, both tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains showed decreased resistance to both CFW and CR relative to the WT strain.

To confirm that the observed phenotypes were attributable to loss of the TPS2 gene, we complemented the tps2Δ strain to generate a TPS2-reintegrant strain (tps2Δ+TPS2). Complementation restored the stress-associated growth phenotypes: thermotolerance returned to WT levels, and resistance to the cell wall stressors CFW and CR was largely indistinguishable from the WT strain (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Tps2 plays a role in echinocandin resistance and tolerance
Given the trehalose biosynthetic pathway is involved in cell wall stress response, we investigated its contribution to resistance against clinically relevant antifungal drugs, which target either the fungal cell membrane (azoles and polyenes) or the cell wall (echinocandins). We conducted drug broth microdilution assays (BDA) (Fig. 2A, B) and ETEST® assays (Fig. 2C) to determine resistance and tolerance towards these drugs.

In this context, reduced relative resistance is interpreted as increased susceptibility compared with the WT strain, while tolerance refers to the ability of a subpopulation of cells to grow slowly but persistently at drug concentrations above the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Together, these assays allowed us to evaluate both resistance and tolerance phenotypes in the trehalose-deficient mutants.

Results from the BDAs revealed that deletion of the TPS2 gene significantly reduced resistance and tolerance to all three echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin). This is evident from respectively lower MIC and reduced growth at concentrations above the MIC (supra-MIC growth), quantified by lower AUC of the BDA (Fig. 2A). RRAUC calculated from the growth curves serve as an indicator of drug tolerance, which is visualized in the heatmap (Fig. 2B). The tps2Δ strain displayed a complete loss of tolerance to all three echinocandins and slightly increased tolerance to fluconazole. Meanwhile, the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains showed a slight increase in tolerance to amphotericin B.

Consistent with the phenotypic observations, Etest analysis demonstrated a clear reduction in echinocandin resistance and tolerance in the tps2Δ strain compared to the WT. The MIC values for all three echinocandins were lower in the tps2Δ strain than in the WT, indicating increased susceptibility. The specific MIC values are shown in the upper right corner of each Etest. Furthermore, the tps2Δ strain exhibited minimal to no growth within the inhibition elipse after 48 h, reflecting a complete loss of echinocandin tolerance (Fig. 2C). In contrast, no significant differences in susceptibility or tolerance to amphotericin B or fluconazole were observed between the tps2Δ and WT strains.

To further establish that the phenotype stems from TPS2 gene loss, we assessed caspofungin susceptibility and tolerance in the TPS2 reintegrant strain (tps2Δ+TPS2) using BDA and Etest assays (Supplementary Fig. S2). Complementation restored WT behavior: the caspofungin MIC of tps2Δ+TPS2 matched WT, and supra-MIC growth was likewise comparable. These results confirm that the heightened echinocandin sensitivity of the tps2Δ strain is due to TPS2 gene deficiency.

T6P accumulation in the tps2Δ strain is independent of caspofungin treatment
To investigate whether intracellular levels of trehalose and T6P influence echinocandin resistance and tolerance in C. auris, we quantified these metabolites in exponentially growing cells, both in the presence and absence of caspofungin (Fig. 3A, B). In unstressed conditions, deletion of the TPS2 gene led to a substantial accumulation of T6P, reaching levels nearly 300-fold higher than those observed in the WT strain. Conversely, deletion of the TPS1 gene, either alone or in combination with the TPS2 gene, resulted in a complete loss of detectable trehalose or T6P. Interestingly, deletion of the TPS2 gene alone still results in low accumulation of a small, residual amount of trehalose, similar to what is observed in C. albicans and C. glabrata31.

To assess whether trehalose or T6P levels respond to echinocandin stress, exponentially growing cells were treated with caspofungin at ten times MIC (2.5 µg/mL) for 60 min. However, no significant changes in trehalose or T6P levels were observed in either the WT or mutant strains following treatment (Fig. 3A, B). It is interesting to note that in the WT under normal conditions, there is already a high amount of trehalose produced. Tps2 exhibits conserved roles across distinct C. auris clades
To assess whether the role of the trehalose synthesis pathway is conserved across different clades of C. auris, we performed a phylogenetic analysis of the Tps2 proteins (Fig. 4A), which revealed that Tps2 is highly conserved across all five C. auris clades, with minimal sequence divergence. To further investigate the functional conservation of the TPS2 gene, we generated TPS2 gene deletion strains in representative strains from Clade III (B11221), Clade IV (B11244), and Clade V (IFRC2087). Clade II was excluded from this analysis, given that Clade II strains are rarely associated with systemic infections and echinocandin treatment35.

The resulting tps2Δ strains from different C. auris clades were analyzed using drug and stress BDAs to assess their responses to diverse antifungal treatments and environmental stresses. From the drug BDA assay (Fig. 4B), all tps2Δ strains exhibited reduced MIC values for three echinocandins compared to their respective WT strain. The stress-response phenotypes observed in these tps2Δ strains were also largely consistent with those observed for the Clade I strain B8441. Specifically, deletion of the TPS2 gene resulted in increased sensitivity to CFW and enhanced resistance to CR, indicating alterations in cell wall stress responses.

To further quantify differences in stress and drug tolerance, relative resistance was assessed by calculating the area under the curve (RRAUC) for each condition (Fig. 4C). Across all clades, tps2Δ strains showed a marked reduction in RRAUC values for echinocandins. For CR stress, RRAUC values increased in all tps2Δ strains, while under CFW stress, RRAUC values decreased, further supporting a shift in cell wall composition and stress response. These findings demonstrate that the function of Tps2 in supporting echinocandin resistance and tolerance and maintaining cell wall integrity is conserved across multiple C. auris clades.

Deletion of the TPS2 gene results in impaired chitin biosynthesis
To investigate the mechanism underlying the increased echinocandin susceptibility of the tps2Δ strain, we compared cell-wall composition in the WT Clade I isolate B8441 and the corresponding panel of Clade I mutant strains. Confocal microscopy was performed to visualize specific components of the cell wall, employing CFW to detect chitin, Alexa Fluor 488–conjugated antibodies to stain β-glucans, and Concanavalin A–Alexa Fluor 488 to visualize mannans (Fig. 5A). In addition, we assessed the expression of genes encoding β-glucan synthases (FKS1 and FKS2) to comprehensively evaluate cell wall biosynthesis alterations in mutant strains (Fig. 6D).

Quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed significant alterations, primarily within the chitin biosynthesis pathway. Collectively, these results are consistent with and support the observed reduction in chitin content specifically observed in the tps2Δ strain.

Gfa1 is essential but does not account for the tps2Δ echinocandin susceptibility
Gene expression assays revealed that GFA1 gene expression was upregulated in the tps2Δ strain. To test this hypothesis, we generated a GFA1 gene knockout strain in the B8441 background and assessed its phenotype using BDA and Etest analysis. Growth curve analysis demonstrated that Gfa1 is essential for viability with glucose as a carbon source in C. auris, as deletion mutants were unable to grow in glucose-containing media (Fig. 7A). The restoration of growth upon supplementation with exogenous glucosamine confirmed that the growth defect was attributable to impaired hexosamine biosynthesis. Notably, when glucosamine was provided at a minimal concentration (10 mM) sufficient to support basal growth, the gfa1Δ strain exhibited substantially reduced resistance and tolerance to caspofungin (Fig. 7B, C). Increasing the concentration of glucosamine progressively improved both resistance and tolerance; however, full recovery to WT levels was not achieved. These findings indicate that the accumulation of T6P does not directly alter the structure or enzymatic function of Gfa1.

T6P accumulation indirectly reduces chitin production by inhibiting hexokinase activity
To investigate how the deletion of the TPS2 gene affects the chitin synthesis pathway, we focused on the role of T6P, a known regulator of the initial steps of glycolysis in yeast, primarily through its inhibition of hexokinase II (Fig. 8A)36. To assess whether this is also the case for C. auris, we analyzed hexokinase enzymatic activity in WT and mutant strains. Both the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains exhibited increased hexokinase activity, while deletion of the TPS2 gene resulted in a significant reduction in hexokinase activity compared to the WT strain (Fig. 8B). Complementation of TPS2 gene restored hexokinase activity to WT levels (Supplementary Fig. S3).

Considering that the trehalose biosynthesis pathway modulates glycolytic flux in various fungal species, we subsequently measured metabolites derived from glucose-dependent pathways. Therefore, 13C NMR spectroscopy was conducted to elucidate the interplay between glycolysis, trehalose metabolism, and chitin synthesis (Fig. 8C–F). The analysis revealed that the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains exhibited an increased and quicker glucose consumption compared to the WT (Fig. 8C). This is similar to what is observed in S. cerevisiae, where a tps1Δ strain has a very high flux into glycolysis because of very high hexokinase activity. As a result of this higher influx in glycolysis, both the tps1Δ and tps1Δ tps2Δ strains produced ethanol at a higher rate compared to the WT (Fig. 8D), while glycerol and mannitol levels remained unchanged (Fig. 8E, F). In contrast, the tps2Δ strain exhibited a pronounced reduction in glucose consumption (Fig. 7C), accompanied by significantly lower levels of glycolysis-derived metabolites, including ethanol, glycerol, and mannitol. As a result, reduced carbon flow through glycolysis may limit the availability of F6P for downstream biosynthetic pathways. Given that UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), the precursor for chitin synthesis, is derived from F6P, these findings also imply that chitin biosynthesis is compromised in the tps2Δ strain. This metabolic constraint likely explains the reduced chitin levels detected in the tps2Δ strain. 13C NMR spectroscopy also confirmed the synthesis of trehalose for the WT and accumulation of T6P for the tps2Δ strain (Supplementary Fig. S4).

Exogenous glucosamine restores caspofungin resistance and tolerance in the tps2Δ strain
To determine whether the reduced resistance and tolerance of the tps2Δ strain to echinocandins were directly attributable to T6P accumulation, resulting in impaired glycolytic flux and subsequently diminished chitin biosynthesis, we performed caspofungin susceptibility assays with varying concentrations of exogenous glucosamine to evaluate its potential to rescue the susceptibility phenotype. The results demonstrated a non-linear relationship between glucosamine concentration and caspofungin resistance. Specifically, the MIC values of the tps2Δ strain were approximately 0.125 µg/mL at 10 mM, 0.25 µg/mL at 20 mM, and 1 µg/mL at both 30 mM and 50 mM glucosamine. These data suggest that low to moderate levels of glucosamine partially restore caspofungin tolerance in the absence of the TPS2 gene (Fig. 9A).

Consistent with the BDA findings, Etest assays performed after 48 h confirmed that glucosamine supplementation improved caspofungin resistance and tolerance in the tps2Δ strain, but this improvement did not continue beyond 30 mM. At both 30 mM and 50 mM glucosamine, the tps2Δ strain exhibited similar capacity for growth within the inhibition ellipse (Fig. 9B). Together, these results suggest that while glucosamine can compensate to some extent for the loss of the TPS2 gene, its ability to enhance caspofungin resistance and tolerance is limited and does not increase indefinitely with concentration.

Deletion of Tps2 sensitizes C. auris to caspofungin in a murine candidemia model
Given the pronounced defects in echinocandin resistance and tolerance observed in the tps2Δ strain under in vitro conditions, we determined whether these phenotypes translated to differences in susceptibility in an in vivo context. To assess the impact of the tps2Δ strain on the in vivo susceptibility of C. auris to caspofungin, immunocompromised mice were intravenously infected with either the WT strain or the tps2Δ strain and subsequently treated with caspofungin or PBS. To assess the virulence of C. auris strains and the therapeutic impact of caspofungin, we measured fungal burden in the kidneys and brains of infected mice, as schematically depicted in Fig. 10A. To assess the health status of mice after infection and treatment, body weight was monitored daily from day 0 to day 6 (Fig. 10B). No significant differences in body weight were observed among the groups, regardless of infection with WT or tps2Δ strains, or treatment with PBS or caspofungin. Further, we found that in the absence of caspofungin treatment, both the WT and tps2Δ strains showed similar levels of fungal burden in these organs, indicating that deletion of the TPS2 gene does not impair the intrinsic virulence of C. auris. However, following caspofungin treatment, fungal burden in mice infected with the tps2Δ cells was significantly lower than in those infected with the WT strain in both kidneys and brains (Fig. 10C). This indicates that tps2Δ cells are less able to survive after caspofungin treatment in vivo. Together, these findings suggest that loss of the TPS2 gene leads to a complete loss of caspofungin tolerance under host conditions and that a combination therapy of echinocandin with a Tps2 inhibitor would be an effective combination therapy.

### Reviewer 3

This tightly reasoned report presents mechanistic insight into the emerging pathogen Candida auris' insensitivity to
echinocandin antifungals. Candida auris has become an increasing menace over the last decade due to its resilience to
antifungals and disinfectants, so on that basis the study is highly significant. Moreover, the findings point to an enzyme with
a causal role, and in this way the authors have a druggable target. This element of the study further increases its
significance.
A second strength of the study is the thoroughness of the analysis. For example, strains from all four major pathogenic C.
auris clades are tested. Also, metabolic inferences are pursued and validated with metabolomic characterization. Finally, a
point that all readers will appreciate is the simplicity of the explanation at which the authors arrive. It is the kind of outcome
that even students in my Introductory Microbiology class could understand and appreciate! In fact, if this work is published in
time, I may even include it in a lecture this fall.
The one minor experimental criticism that I have is that the most revealing mutant, the tps2Δ strain, was not complemented.
There was a G418 marker developed by Santana and O'Meara in Nat Commun. 2021 Dec 10;12(1):7197 that might be
useful, or the authors could recycle their NAT marker as they do for other purposes. I do not doubt the overall
phenotypic results as they stand - the authors make the mutant in multiple strains, for example - but for some of the findings,
such as reduced chitin accumulation and reduced hexokinase activity, complementation would ensure that the conclusions reach the
highest standard.
The one minor manuscript preparation criticism that I have is that the Discussion and Results sections seem to overlap more
than necessary. I wondered if the authors might benefit from merging the two into a single "Results and Discussion" format.
This issue is more of a matter of taste though, which is why I consider it quite minor.
My one strong recommendation with regard to manuscript preparation is that the authors should define clearly what
resistance and tolerance each mean. These are terms with distinctions that can be a little hazy among a broad audience. I
am 99% certain that the authors' assays are completely in line with the simple definitions that I always refer to
(Berman and Krysan, Nat Rev Microbiol. 2020 Jun;18(6):319-331), so I do not question the authors' assays and conclusions;
my recommendation is really to make sure the work can be appreciated by a broad readership.
